And with one of Miro's ready-made templates, you can go from discovery and research to product roadmap to customer journey flows to final mocks. You get the picture. Head on over to miro.com/lenny, leave your suggestions. That's M-I-R-O.com/lenny. (00:41:05): I feel like being a PM is such a thankless job so often and these are what you live for as a PM. It's just like these success stories.
turns.zh: 本期节目由Miro赞助，这款在线视觉白板专为像你我这样的团队设计。我有个小请求，请前往miro.com/lenny查看我的白板，并告诉我你希望我在2023年邀请哪位嘉宾。访问Miro白板时，欢迎随意探索。这是一个绝佳的共享空间，能与同事紧密协作，快速捕捉创意、获取反馈并迭代项目。（00:40:30）例如，在Miro中，你可以通过便利贴头脑风暴构建产品策略，添加评论、实时反应和投票工具，甚至使用估算应用规划团队冲刺。整个分布式团队可以围绕线框图展开合作，用笔工具绘制创意，或直接在Miro白板上制作模型。借助Miro的现成模板，你可以从探索研究到产品路线图，再到客户旅程流图，最终完成模型设计。总之，你懂的。请前往miro.com/lenny留下你的建议。网址是M-I-R-O.com/lenny。（00:41:05）我觉得产品经理这份工作常常得不到应有的认可，而这些成功案例正是我们作为PM的意义所在。

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: Absolutely. One of the things that was unexpected when I started at Tinder was a couple times a week I would meet someone or I'd be in an Uber and the Uber driver would tell me, people would share like, "Oh, I met my boyfriend or girlfriend, or I met my wife or my husband on the platform." And it was really great to hear the stories. One of the things I didn't realize is the degree to which because of Tinder's very lightweight designs, it's been able to support the LGBTQ community much better than other dating products. And so some of my most fulfilling conversations with people who felt like they wouldn't have met their significant other without Tinder because there was just no place to do that.
turns.zh: 没错。我刚加入Tinder时，最意外的事情之一就是，每周总有几次我会遇到新朋友，或者在优步车上听到司机分享他们的故事，比如“哦，我在平台上遇到了男朋友/女朋友，或者找到了另一半”。听这些故事真的很棒。但我之前没意识到，由于Tinder的设计非常简洁，它比其他交友产品更好地支持了LGBTQ群体。其中一些最让我感动的对话，是那些觉得如果没有Tinder就遇不到另一半的人——因为他们根本没有其他相遇的平台。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, man. Fulfilling, impactful, interesting, surprising. What a role. Actually met my wife online on a defunct dating site app called howaboutwe.com. Do you remember that one at all?
turns.zh: 哇，真令人惊喜。太有意义了，也太有影响力了。这真是了不起的成就。实际上，我是在一个已经下线的交友应用howaboutwe.com上认识我妻子的。你还记得那个平台吗？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: No. I haven't even heard that.
turns.zh: 不记得了。我甚至都没听说过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It was too good. It just matches people. It's like it reached Hinge's vision too well where they just... nobody needed to stay on. We don't just spend a lot of time on it, but basically the concept was how about we? And it's like a date concept. So instead of browsing profiles, you browse date ideas and then you say, "Hey, I want to do this date with you and let's go out and try it out." And it worked out for us.
turns.zh: 那个平台太棒了。它能精准匹配用户。它甚至超越了Hinge的愿景——Hinge的理念是让用户无需长期停留在平台上。我们虽然没在上面花太多时间，但核心概念就是“那要不约个会？”然后用户可以浏览各种约会创意，接着说“嘿，我想和你一起尝试这个约会”，结果我们就成功了。

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: That's really cool. There's so much opportunity. I think there's a lot of really good dating ideas that haven't been explored yet.
turns.zh: 太酷了。有太多的机会了。我觉得还有很多优秀的交友理念尚未被探索。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm. Interesting. All right. Good investment tip. Coming back to the product stack, getting back on track. One interesting thing about your product stack that's a little bit contrarian is you put goals after roadmap. And I'm curious why that is? Why you think goals should come after having a roadmap?
turns.zh: 嗯，有意思。好的，我再问个问题。关于产品路线图，你把目标放在路线图之后，这有点与众不同。为什么会这样？你为什么认为目标应该在路线图之后呢？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: Yeah, it's definitely a contrarian point of view. I've had a few people yell at me about this. Typically, what happens is goals are almost the start of a strategic process rather than the end of it. A company will say, "We need to increase our revenue by X, or we need to increase our retention by Y. What's our strategy to be able to do that?" And what I've found over the years is that that goals first approach puts the entire energy of the product team on moving the goals without any sort of structure of what success looks like and why. (00:43:17): The analogy I like to use, it's a little bit like taking a road trip and starting out by saying, "Hey, we need to drive 250 miles." It's like, no, if you're going to take a road trip, you first decide where you want to drive to. If you're in LA, you might take a road trip to Vegas. And so our destination is Vegas, and we'll know whether or not we reach there if we've driven 250 miles. Because that 250-mile goal is in the context of a destination. (00:43:42): And so I think about all of the pieces of the strategy stack as being really clear about what is the end destination that you're solving for, and then you should work on goals to the extent that they help you reach that destination. And if you find that achieving your goal is actually pulling away from the destination, then there's a really important conversation to be had about do we leave that gain on the table because it's not aligned with our destination, or do we need to change our destination? And I think what happens too often when people start with goals and then create the roadmap is that the goal takes precedence and there's no context, there's no principles that are ultimately driving that. And so those decisions about the direction of the product come and go without even really being noticed because there's nothing to calibrate against.
turns.zh: 是的，这绝对是一个反主流观点。我曾为此被不少人指责过。通常来说，目标几乎是战略进程的起点，而非终点。一家公司会说：“我们需要将收入提升X，或者将客户留存率提高Y。那么，我们该如何实现这些目标呢？” 多年来我发现，这种先设定目标的做法会让产品团队把全部精力都投入到达成目标上，而缺乏对成功定义及原因的系统思考。（00:43:17）：我常用的一个比喻是，类似于开启一次公路旅行时先说：“嘿，我们需要开250英里。”但不行，若要开启公路旅行，首先要确定目的地。如果你在洛杉矶，或许会选择去拉斯维加斯。我们的目的地是拉斯维加斯，而250英里是否能抵达那里取决于目的地的设定。（00:43:42）：因此，我认为战略体系的各个环节都必须清晰：你要解决的终极目标是什么？然后，你应当根据目标来制定达成该目标的路径。如果发现达成目标的过程偏离了终极目标，那么就需要认真思考：是放弃这个目标，因为它与终极目标不符，还是调整终极目标？我认为很多时候，人们先设定目标再制定路线图时，往往会让目标凌驾于终极目标之上，缺乏最终驱动目标的框架和原则。因此，关于产品方向的决策往往来来去去，却鲜少得到审视。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I a hundred percent agree that strategy should come ahead of goals. What's interesting is, so if your approach is strategy then figure out what you're building and then figure out your goals, how do you prioritize the roadmap? Because from my perspective, come up with your strategy how are we going to get to where we're going to get. Goals to me are how we measure progress towards that. And then the roadmap comes out of what's going to help us achieve this goal, and how do we prioritize based on what's going to most impact this goal that we have. So how do you approach prioritizing and picking what's going to be in the roadmap if you don't have your goals? Is it more like, here's the main KPI, or you have a rough sense of KPIs and metrics you're going to watch and use that to prioritize? Or how do you think about that?
turns.zh: 所以我完全认同战略应当先于目标。有趣的是，如果你的方法是先制定战略，再明确要建设的产品，最后设定目标，那么路线图的优先级该如何排序？从我的角度来看，先制定战略——我们将如何抵达目标？对我来说，目标是衡量实现目标进展的指标。然后，路线图应基于有助于达成目标的因素，并根据对目标影响最大的因素进行优先级排序。那么，若没有明确的目标，该如何确定路线图的优先级呢？是以主要KPI为导向？还是大致确定要监控的KPI和指标，并以此为依据进行优先级排序？你又如何看待这个问题？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: Yeah, I think as part of the strategy, you'll typically have some quantifiable elements of that strategy. So for example, for Tripadvisor, our strategy was with trip planning, we wanted people to come directly to Tripadvisor and spend more time on Tripadvisor. And so what was happening was that most of a person's usage of Tripadvisor was interleaved with visits to Google. And so people would search for something, Boston hotels, come to Tripadvisor. They might say, "No, I want to look at New York." They Google New York hotels, and they come and look at Tripadvisor. And Tripadvisor's in a really good position to actually not have a person go back to Google because we knew about the preferences, we knew about their states, we knew who else they might be traveling with. And so more of that planning activity could happen directly within the product. (00:46:01): And so the problem was that at a company like Tripadvisor, which is very experimental, very quantitatively focused, the product teams were constantly optimizing for what's going to drive bookings in the moment. And so the thing that drives bookings from a visit to Google naturally moves a person down a transaction path and gets them to the booking and doesn't have them stop along the way to set up their trip and start to add things to their trip and create their wishlist. That actually gets in the way of the transaction itself. And so in the absence of that strategy around, we actually want to get people to come directly to Tripadvisor more often. We were doing so many things that ultimately undermined that strategy and got people to sort of leapfrog through the product instead of stay with the product. (00:46:50): And so that's a really good example of where if we know we want to generate that long-term continuous relationship with the user, there's a set of things from a roadmap standpoint that we can do to do that. We can prioritize those things, we can use numbers, we can opportunity size them, we can prioritize based on that, and then we can measure whether or not we're made progress based on that strategic and very conceptual understanding of where we want to go.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为作为战略的一部分，通常会有一些可量化的元素。以猫途鹰（Tripadvisor）为例，我们的战略是围绕旅行规划展开的，希望用户能直接访问猫途鹰并在平台上停留更久。然而，用户使用猫途鹰的过程中，往往会频繁切换到谷歌搜索。比如，用户搜索“波士顿酒店”后，可能会跳转到猫途鹰，但又会被引导回谷歌继续搜索纽约酒店。猫途鹰原本有很好的机会留住用户，因为我们掌握了用户的偏好、旅行状态和同行伙伴信息，但由于产品团队过于关注短期转化目标，导致用户无法专注于规划行程，最终流失了大量潜在客户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the biggest takeaway I think we both fully agree on is your strategy should come ahead of having goals and coming up with your goals and aligning on goals. No question. (00:47:25): Speaking of goals, you also have some really interesting insights on just how to come up with goals and best practices for aligning and setting goals. I'd love to dig into that a little bit and then I have another topic I want to talk about.
turns.zh:
所以，我认为我们都深有共识：战略必须先于目标设定，之后才能制定具体目标并达成共识。这是毫无疑问的。（00:47:25）  
说到目标设定，你在如何制定目标以及如何有效达成目标方面有很多深刻见解。我很想深入探讨这个话题，然后再聊聊其他内容。

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: Yeah, that sounds good. So I've done a little bit of writing about goals, which came out of... I've been at multiple companies that have put OKRs into practice and had a really hard time with that. And I've talked to a lot of product teams who have had a hard time. So the question I started asking is, why are companies having a hard time with OKRs? What's happening that is preventing teams from being able to set goals that they really understand how to achieve and achieving those goals? (00:48:01): And one of the things that I found, which I think was sort of a first principle that's happening at a lot of companies, is this idea of always focusing on outcomes over outputs and comes from a good place, which is ultimately, and I think this is the case, ultimately, a PM needs to measure their success based on whether or not they generate valuable outcomes for the business. But that doesn't necessarily mean that in this quarter we need to commit to a specific outcome or that we should commit to a specific outcome that we may or may not know how to move. (00:48:33): And so I think ultimately the goal is to drive outcomes, but oftentimes there's things that come before that that need to be addressed ahead of time so that you can really understand what the plan for meeting those outcomes is going to look like. And so I refer to that as the frontier of understanding. There's a point at which what the team knows and what the team doesn't know. There's a junction point there, which is this frontier. And it could be actually we don't know what moves retention. If you ask me to remove retention, I can brainstorm 10 experiments, but I don't actually know why people are continuing to use our product. And so then it doesn't make sense to commit to a retention goal because you're going to sort of throw a spaghetti against the wall, have a bunch of experiments, [inaudible 00:49:16] will stick, and maybe you'll be able to move the metric, but you won't have understood exactly why, or you might move the metric in a way that is not tied to the strategy that you have as a business. (00:49:27): So the first type of risk is really understanding risk. And if you don't understand how to move a particular metric, then the right goal is to set a goal to increase your understanding not to move that metric. Once you have an understanding of how to move the metric, your team may or may not be able to execute very well. It might not be able to execute those sorts of experiments. It may not have the resources that it needs to execute. And so then you might want to set an execution goal. So we want to hit 20 experiments this quarter, and if you can hit those 20 experiments, you'll know that you're executing really, really well. And even if those experiments don't work, that moves that frontier a little bit forward. (00:50:04): And then finally the ultimate frontier is strategic risk. We understand how to move retention or we think we understand how to move retention. We're going to do a set of things to do that. And then either we'll learn that our understanding is correct, in which case we can pull that lever more, or we'll learn that it's not correct, in which case we need to go back to understanding and goal ourselves based on that.
turns.zh:
是啊，这听起来不错。所以我写了一些关于目标设定的文章，这些想法源于……我曾在多家实施OKR的公司工作，发现实施起来困难重重。我还与许多产品团队交流过，他们也遇到了同样的挑战。因此，我开始思考一个问题：为什么这么多公司在OKR实施上困难重重？究竟是什么因素导致团队无法设定切实可行的目标并最终达成这些目标？（00:48:01）  

我发现的一个核心问题，也是许多公司普遍存在的误区，是始终关注结果而非产出。这种理念出发点是好的，毕竟项目经理最终需要根据是否为业务创造了有价值的结果来衡量成功。但这并不意味着我们必须在本季度承诺达成某个具体结果，或者强制设定一个可能实现也可能无法实现的目标。（00:48:33）  

所以我认为，最终目标是推动结果的实现，但往往在此之前需要先解决一些前置问题。比如，团队对某个结果的理解程度如何？团队是否存在未知的领域？这就是“理解的前沿”。当团队对某个领域知之甚少时，就需要提前探索。这正是需要突破的边界。例如，团队可能不清楚如何提升用户留存率。如果你让我去提升留存率，我能想出10个实验方案，但我根本不清楚用户为何持续使用我们的产品。因此，盲目设定留存率目标是没有意义的，因为这无异于碰运气——可能其中某个实验能带来微弱改善，但却与业务战略脱节。（00:49:27）  

所以，第一类风险是理解风险。如果团队不清楚如何提升某个指标，那么正确的做法应该是设定提升理解能力的目标，而不是强制达成指标。一旦团队理解了如何提升指标，团队可能执行不力——缺乏执行实验的资源和能力。这种情况下，可以设定执行目标，比如本季度完成20个实验。即使实验失败，也能推动理解边界前移。（00:50:04）  

最后，终极边界是战略风险。我们理解了如何提升留存率，或者自认为理解了如何提升。但实际操作过程中，要么验证自己的理解是正确的，可以进一步推进；要么发现理解有误，需要回归理解，重新设定目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really interesting. So the term is frontier of understanding, right?
turns.zh: 这真的很有趣。那么“理解的前沿”这个术语，是对吧？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And there's four buckets that you just described of types of goals. Can you repeat them again?
turns.zh: 您刚才提到的四种目标类型，您能再复述一遍吗？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: Yeah. So the four buckets are, it starts with understanding risk, which is we have something that we want to do but we don't really understand what the levers are. Then the next thing is dependency risk, which is we understand what we think the levers are, but we may or may not have the tools that we need in order to make progress. Then there's execution risk, which is we have all the resources that we need, we have a really strong hypothesis, and then we may or may not be able to execute against those hypotheses. And the last thing is strategic risk, which is we have a hypothesis and it might turn out that that was not the right hypothesis.
turns.zh: 好的。这四种类型分别是：首先是理解风险，即我们想做某件事，但不清楚关键影响因素；接下来是依赖风险，即我们知道影响因素，但可能缺乏推进所需的工具；然后是执行风险，即我们具备所有资源，有明确的假设，但能否成功执行尚存不确定；最后是战略风险，即我们的假设可能最终被证明是错误的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man. I wanted to move on to a different topic, but I want to dig into this a little bit because it's really interesting. So a lot of people work at companies where their product manager, leader is not going to be like, "Cool, let's spend a quarter understanding if we can move this metric." That seems like you have to be a really evolved leader to be okay with that, or is that even not a good idea to spend a quarter doing that? How do you think about not actually having a goal that is moving a metric that people care about and focusing on understanding and kind of pushing this frontier of understanding further versus just moving a metric that people actually want you to move?
turns.zh: 天哪。我本想转到下一个话题，但这个话题实在太有意思了。很多公司里的产品经理或领导者不会说：“好的，我们花一个季度时间去了解是否能提升这个指标。”要做到这点，领导者得非常开明才行，或者说，这样做根本不明智吧？您怎么看待这种情况：如果没有一个能推动人们关心的指标的目标，而是专注于理解和突破认知边界，而非简单地去提升一个现有指标？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: It might be that for the quarter, the way that the company works, the things that it's focused on. You need to actually commit to a goal to move retention or a goal to move your follower count or something like that. There's two ways to do that. One is you can commit to that goal and then in three months kind of hope for the best and just do a lot of work that you think might actually move the lever. The other thing is to say actually that journey towards hitting that particular goal, we can break into. Initially let's spend a couple of weeks understanding. We'll talk to customers. We'll do some analysis. We'll form some really good hypotheses. And then based on those hypotheses we'll start to figure out what do we need to execute on in order to start to validate those hypotheses. And then we can execute on those things and validate those hypotheses. (00:52:28): And depending on where in the quarter things start to go off the rails, you'll have a feeling for where that frontier is. And when you miss the goal, you can then go back to the team or the leadership and say, "We missed our goal, but I think I know why. Here's the things that we did within the quarter and here's where things started to go off the rails. Here's what I'd suggest that we commit to for the next quarter so that we can be much more sure that we're going to hit our goal." (00:52:50): And leadership is always going to be outcome driven, but they also want to have a lot of confidence that we're going to be able to hit those outcomes. And so if you can clearly convey the learning and provide a really clear path that will get them that confidence, they're often going to be much more [inaudible 00:53:07] than you anticipate. I think the desire to always set outcome-based goals is just shorthand for we want you to move the needle and we want you to be thinking about that. That doesn't mean that you do that in the absence of really detailed understanding and really honing your execution process so that you can execute flawlessly. So approaching things in that way can help you change the conversation and make it much more specific.
turns.zh: 可能是由于本季度公司的运作方式以及其关注的重点所在。你需要真正致力于某个目标，比如提升用户留存率、增加粉丝数量之类的。实现这一目标有两种方法。一种是设定目标，然后在三个月内寄希望于最好的结果，同时开展大量你认为可能推动进展的工作。另一种方法是分解实现目标的路径。首先，花几周时间进行理解。我们会与客户沟通，进行分析，形成合理的假设。然后基于这些假设，确定需要采取哪些行动来验证这些假设。接着实施这些行动，并验证假设。（00:52:28）：根据季度进展中可能出现偏差的情况，你就能清楚界限所在。当未能达成目标时，可以向团队或领导层汇报：“我们未能达成目标，但我认为原因在于……”。接着列出季度内采取的措施、偏差产生的环节，并提出下季度需重点推进的方向。（00:52:50）：领导层始终以结果为导向，但他们也希望对达成目标充满信心。因此，若能清晰传达学习成果，并提供明确的路径来获取这种信心，他们往往会比你预期的更积极支持。我认为设定基于结果的目标，实质上是希望你推动进展并持续思考。但这并不意味着在缺乏深入理解和优化执行流程的情况下就能轻松达成目标。因此，以这种方式处理问题能帮助你转变对话重点，使讨论更具针对性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you also have a post about this exact topic, right?
turns.zh: 你还有一篇关于这个主题的文章，对吧？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: I do, yeah. I've got a post on the Reforge blog. Can't remember the title. I think it's Set Better Goal with NCTs instead of OKRs.
turns.zh: 是的，我在Reforge博客上写过一篇文章。标题记不清了。好像是《用NCTs而非OKRs设定更优目标》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. So if your manager is not buying what you're saying, that could be interesting to share with them and see if that'll change their mind. Your first point is worst case, you just hope for the best. You know that your frontier understanding is not that far, but still set that ambitious outcome-based goal and then hopefully works out. But in reality, it may not be realistic.
turns.zh: 好的，不错。如果你的经理不认同你的观点，可以分享这篇文章看看能否改变他们的看法。你的第一个观点是，退一步说，你只能寄希望于最好的结果。你知道对目标的理解还不够深入，但还是设定了雄心勃勃的基于结果的目标，然后祈祷能成功。但实际上，这可能不现实。

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: I think we can think about it as two by two matrix. On one axis of the matrix you have, did we hit our goals? And on the other access we have, do we know why? And ultimately you want to be in the upper right quadrant. You want to hit your goals and know why you hit your goals. Some teams are in the quadrant where they hit their goals, but they don't know why, which is good for now, but it's eventually going to catch up with you. And then an important thing to be in is if you didn't hit your goals to make sure that you're at least understanding why or at least you're making progress on understanding why. And I think too often teams get so focused on the goals, they get less focused on the learning.
turns.zh: 我认为我们可以将其视为一个二维矩阵。在矩阵的一轴上，你要问自己：我们是否达到了目标？在另一轴上，你要问自己：我们是否清楚达成目标的原因？最终，你希望自己的位置处于右上象限——既达成目标，又能解释达成目标的原因。有些团队虽然达成了目标，但却不清楚原因。这在短期内或许无伤大雅，但最终必将自食其果。若未能达成目标，关键在于确保至少能理解其中的原因，或者至少在理解原因的道路上有所进展。我发现很多团队过于专注于目标，却忽视了学习的重要性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, final topic, product management competencies. So this is a post you wrote a while ago. It's the post I've shared most of your many writings online, and I'm going to pull up this image on my screen. So another plug to check it out on YouTube or Spotify. Can you talk about what this is and why it's important for PMs to think of their career in this view and in general just understand what the components of a great PM are?
turns.zh: 好的，最后一个话题——产品管理能力。这是你不久前写的一篇文章，也是我在网上分享过你众多作品中最多的一篇。我现在要把这张图片展示在屏幕上。再推荐一下，你可以在YouTube或Spotify上查看相关内容。能否谈谈这篇文章的内容，以及为什么产品经理需要从这个视角看待自己的职业生涯？总的来说，能否解释一下成为一名优秀产品经理所需的核心要素？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: Yeah, definitely. So we developed this at Tripadvisor. When I joined Tripadvisor, the company was newly public and as part of being a newly public company and wanted to grow different teams really quickly including the product team. And what we were finding is that hiring a product out of industry, and at the time we were based in Boston. So hiring a really good experience PM in Boston was taking between three and six months, and that just was too long to reach the sort of growth goals that we wanted to hit from a team perspective and a headcount perspective. (00:55:34): And so the head of product there came up with this program called the product rotational program, where we would hire people directly out of business school and out of undergrad into their first product role regardless of whether or not they had prior product experience. And they would go through two years of rotations. So four six-month rotations where they would be able to focus on teams that are zero to one teams or growth teams or infrastructure teams. So the goal was in about two years to get a person to be able to experience various different parts of product management and have them come out with the skills to be a senior and effective product manager. (00:56:12): And so as part of that, we really needed to define very clearly what is product management and how do we help people identify the skills that they need to be an effective product manager and give them a plan so that they can grow those skills. And so that's how this framework initially came to be. The framework consists of 12 competencies in four different areas. These competencies I think are the same for APMs as they are for CPOs, and I can talk a little bit about how they change as a person gets more senior. But these 12 areas are equally important regardless of where you are within your product management journey. The specifics might change, but the overlying structure remains the same. (00:56:51): The first thing that's really important is product execution. So PMs need to be able to work with their teams to build product, and that breaks down into three sub-competencies. The first is functional specification. So that's the ability to work with your team to define what is the PRD or the functional specification that defines what you want to build. The second thing is product delivery, which is the ability to work with engineering and design and the other teams to take that specification and turn it into working product. And the third piece, which I've changed from quality assurance is now product quality, is making sure that what you build is high quality, not just from a technical perspective, but also from a design perspective, a usability perspective and a business perspective. (00:57:34): And so ultimately that's the foundation of being a successful product manager is being able to execute. And that's as true for an APM as it is for a VP or a CPO. An APM is going to think about product execution in terms of their day-to-day individual contribution. But a CPO is going to think about product execution in terms of the systems that they create to enable teams to define really good specifications, to deliver products really effectively, to execute flawlessly and to deliver products that have a very high bar of quality. (00:58:04): The second area is customer insight. So in addition to being able to build products, you need to understand customers so you can figure out what to build. The three subcomponents here are fluency with data, which is the ability to use all of the data at your fingertips to make decisions about what customers need. The second one is voice of the customer, which is the ability to have the conversations with the customer so that the product manager can be the advocate for the customer throughout the entire company as well as the advocate within the product. (00:58:31): The third is user experience design. And so this goes back to our earlier conversation about wireframes. I think a fundamental part of being a really good product manager is the ability to think about the user experience in a very detailed way to make sure that you're not just defining functionality, but you're really clearly understanding how that functionality turns into user experience. And this is very explicitly user experience design and not user interface design because the experience of your product may vary. If you're building APIs, then your experience is actually the API spec. If you're building ML models, then your experience might be the training models or the other systems that you're using to identify the effectiveness of those training models. So this can be a skill that you can think about really broadly across a lot of different product roles. (00:59:17): The third piece is product strategy, and that breaks down into three things. The first one is being able to own business outcomes. So it's really important to move away from thinking about product as shipping features to driving business outcomes. And so this competency is about understanding how does your product or the features that you're working on plug into the business and drive value for the business. The next competency is product vision and road mapping. So that's the ability to take the individual pieces of work that you're doing for a product and put those together into a coherent vision and roadmap that allows you to build towards the product strategy and the company strategy over time. The third one is strategic impact. You're just like product road mapping as a sequence of features. I think about strategic impact as a sequence of business outcomes. So initially [inaudible 01:00:08] really focused on owning business outcomes and delivering business outcomes. But ultimately what's really important is does that sequence of business outcomes move the strategy forward and help you deliver impact on that strategy? (01:00:21): And then the fourth and final piece is all about leadership. So it's influencing people. The first up competency is stakeholder inclusion, so that's being able to work with all of the different people throughout your organization to rally them around the work that you're doing. The second one is team leadership. This is one that doesn't actually come into play until you have direct reports, but once you have direct reports, being able to help those direct reports become really great product managers is a critical skill. And the last one, which is always really important for PMs, is being able to manage up so that you can win the support of the leadership within your organization.
turns.zh:
是的，当然。我们在TripAdvisor开发了这个项目。当我加入TripAdvisor时，这家公司刚刚上市，作为一家新上市的公司，我们希望快速壮大各个团队，包括产品团队。但我们发现，从行业外招聘产品经理非常困难——当时我们总部位于波士顿，在波士顿招聘一位优秀的产品体验经理需要三到六个月的时间，而这对实现团队和人员规模的增长目标来说实在太慢了。（00:55:34）于是产品负责人提出了"产品轮岗计划"，专门招募刚从商学院或本科毕业的学生，让他们直接进入产品经理岗位，无论是否有产品经验。通过为期两年的轮岗——每次六个月——他们可以深入零到一团队、增长团队或基础设施团队。目标是在两年内让这些新人掌握产品管理的各个方面，成长为资深且高效的产品经理。（00:56:12）为此，我们必须清晰定义什么是产品管理，以及如何帮助人们识别成为高效产品经理所需的技能。我们由此开发了这个框架。框架包含四个领域的12项能力。我认为这些能力对APM和CPO同样适用，但随着职级提升，侧重点会发生变化。不过无论处于产品管理生涯的哪个阶段，这12项能力都同样重要。具体细节可能有所调整，但核心结构保持不变。（00:56:51）首要核心能力是产品执行。产品经理需要与团队合作开发产品，具体分为三项子能力：第一项是功能规范，即与团队共同定义PRD或功能规范；第二项是产品交付，即与工程、设计等团队将规范转化为可用的产品；第三项是产品质量（替代原有的质量保证），确保产品不仅技术过硬，还在设计、可用性和商业价值方面达到高标准。（00:57:34）产品执行是成功产品经理的基石，无论是APM、VP还是CPO都必须具备这一能力。APM关注个人日常贡献中的产品执行，而CPO则专注于搭建系统，帮助团队制定优质规范、高效交付产品、确保无缝执行并交付高质量成果。（00:58:04）第二核心能力是客户洞察。除了产品开发，还需理解客户需求以明确产品方向。子能力包括数据流畅性（利用现有数据）和客户洞察（理解用户需求）。
做出关于客户需求的决策。第二个是"客户之声"，即与客户进行对话的能力，这样产品经理就能在整个公司内为客户发声，同时在产品团队内部也充当客户的代言人。（00:58:31）：第三个是用户体验设计。这又回到了我们之前关于线框图的讨论。我认为，成为一名优秀的产品经理的关键在于能够以非常细致的方式思考用户体验，确保你不仅定义了功能，还清楚理解这些功能如何转化为用户体验。这显然属于用户体验设计，而非用户界面设计，因为产品的体验可能因场景而异。如果你开发的是API，那么用户体验实际上就是API规范；如果你开发的是机器学习模型，那么用户体验可能是训练模型或用于评估这些模型有效性的其他系统。因此，这项技能可以广泛应用于许多不同的产品角色。（00:59:17）：第三个部分是产品战略，它可分为三个方面。第一个是能够主导业务成果。关键在于从只专注于产品功能的交付转向推动业务成果。因此，这项能力需要理解你的产品或正在开发的功能如何融入业务，为业务创造价值。接下来是产品愿景和路线图规划。这意味着能够将你为产品所做的各个工作环节整合成一个连贯的愿景和路线图，逐步实现产品战略和公司战略。第三个是战略影响。你可以将产品路线图视为一系列功能的序列，而战略影响则是一系列业务成果的序列。因此，最初你可能专注于主导业务成果的交付，但最终更重要的是，这一系列业务成果是否能推动战略前进，并帮助你对该战略产生影响？（01:00:21）：最后一个部分是领导力。即影响他人。第一个能力是利益相关者参与，这意味着能够与组织内的不同人员合作，让他们团结在你所做的工作周围。第二个是团队领导力。这项能力通常在你有直接下属后才会发挥作用，但一旦有了直接下属，帮助他们成为优秀的产品经理是一项关键技能。最后一点，对产品经理始终非常重要的是向上管理，以赢得组织内领导层的支持。

If you're a growth PM, you might have a certain focus that might include a lot of focus on data and outcome ownership. If you're more of a product discovery or product innovation PM, you may have a different set of skills. So being able to map yourself out. We'll help you understand where you want to grow and what types of roles are a really good fit for you.
turns.zh: 是的，绝对如此。在我的网站上，我提供了一个可下载的工具包，里面有自我评估的工具。它更详细地介绍了每个能力模块，还探讨了不同的产品经理角色原型。比如，你会发现不同类型的产品经理拥有不同的能力集群。如果你是一名增长型产品经理，可能更注重数据和结果负责；如果你是产品探索或创新型产品经理，所需技能则有所不同。通过自我测评，你能清晰了解自己的发展方向，以及哪些角色最适合你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Plug the site while you're at it. Where do they find this exactly?
turns.zh: 顺便宣传一下网站。用户具体在哪里能找到这些内容？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: They can find it at ravi-mehta.com. So M-E-H-T-A.
turns.zh: 他们可以在ravi-mehta.com找到。网址是M-E-H-T-A。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. You have this kind of concept of exponential feedback that kind of relates to this and just partly touches on why this is so important for PMs to think about. Can you talk a bit about that?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你提到的指数级反馈概念与此相关，也部分解释了为什么产品经理需要重视这一点。能否详细讲讲？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: Yeah, definitely. So this is something we talked about in the product leadership program. One of the most challenging things I think for both a PM as well as a product leader is to figure out how to grow yourself and grow your team. And a key way to do that is through feedback. It's really important to provide people with good feedback to help them understand how to grow. But the problem is, and this is true in a casual one-on-one, as much as it's true in an annual performance review, it's oftentimes the feedback that people provide is very surface level. It may focus on particular symptoms but not root causes. (01:02:53): And so one of the ways that this framework can help is, I'll often encourage people when they're first starting to use the framework, just to go through each competency and rate themselves needs focus, on track or outperforming on each of the competencies to quickly get a read on where you feel like you're landing. You can ask your manager to do that same thing. You can do that in five or 10 minutes. And then the areas where your manager and you see eye to eye and the areas where you guys see differently is stimulus for a really deep conversation. (01:03:25): And so I think that is like the entry point to providing exponential feedback. And I think about exponential feedback as feedback that has compounding returns. So if you give someone feedback on a particular symptom or you give them feedback on something that's tactical and they fix that in a moment, the feedback, the conclusion of that feedback, it just happens and then it's gone. But if instead you help a person understand the underlying behaviors that led to that particular situation, then they can focus on growing themselves. They can also focus on helping to diagnose their own performance more effectively, and that leads to compounding returns where they just keep getting better and better over time. [NEW_PARAGRAPH]And so the ability to kind of apply the competencies as a lens helps you move out of that abstract, kind of surface level feedback into very specific categorizations of things that a person might need to work on, which I think gets to the root cause of areas a person can grow in and that ultimately leads to more effective feedback that has those compounding returns.
turns.zh:
是的，绝对没错。这正是我们在产品领导力项目中探讨的内容。我认为，无论是产品经理还是产品负责人，最具挑战性的事情之一，就是如何提升自己和团队的成长能力。而获取反馈正是实现这一目标的关键途径。为员工提供有效的反馈，帮助他们明确成长方向至关重要。但问题在于，无论是在随意的一对一交流中，还是在年度绩效评估中，人们提供的反馈往往流于表面，仅关注具体问题而忽视深层根源。（01:02:53）  

这个框架能发挥作用的方式之一是，当人们刚开始使用这个框架时，我通常会鼓励他们逐一评估每个能力项，自我评定在这些能力上是需要改进、进展顺利还是表现出色。这样能快速了解自身的成长现状。可以让你的经理也进行同样的评估，用五到十分钟就能完成。然后观察你们在哪些方面看法一致，哪些方面存在分歧，这将为深入对话提供契机。（01:03:25）  

我认为这就是提供指数级反馈的切入点。指数级反馈指的是能产生复合效益的反馈。例如，如果你仅针对某个症状或战术性问题提供反馈，而对方很快就能改正，那这种反馈的效果可能转瞬即逝。但如果你能帮助对方理解导致该问题的深层行为模式，他们就能专注于自我提升，并更有效地诊断自身表现。这种反馈会产生复合效益，随着时间推移，他们会不断进步。  

将这些能力项作为评估框架，能帮助你从抽象的表面反馈转向具体的成长方向，直击个人提升的核心根源，最终提供能产生复合效益的有效反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On that thread, just maybe a last question here. If your manager isn't good at this and isn't giving you this sort of feedback, do you have any advice for how to get feedback from people like this, mentors, anything like that? If your manager just kind of isn't doing that, isn't filling that role for you.
turns.zh: 关于这个话题，最后再问一个问题。如果你的经理不擅长提供这类反馈，你有没有什么建议如何从导师或其他人那里获得反馈？如果你的经理没有承担起这个角色，没有提供有效的反馈，你该如何应对？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: One of the things you can do if you are in a product role is ask them to do this exercise and evaluate you. Your manager will almost certainly have some impression of your performance that they haven't necessarily... If they're not doing it proactively, they probably have it intuitively. And helping them get it down on paper and getting it more specific can be a really good way to start that conversation. So that's one thing that you can do. (01:05:06): A second thing is I think oftentimes people refrain from giving feedback when they feel like that feedback is going to be intrusive. So just inviting your manager to say, "Look, I'm really looking to level up. Please give me feedback whenever you see something. You can give it to me in real time. Don't worry about wordsmithing it. I just want to make sure that I'm getting better." That agreement with your manager and giving them permission to give you that feedback will make sure that the stream of feedback has a much higher volume and starting with the quantity of feedback as a way to get eventually to quality of feedback as well.
turns.zh: 如果你身处产品岗位，有一件事可以做，那就是请他们参与这个练习并对你的表现进行评估。你的经理几乎肯定对你的工作表现有一些印象，但他们不一定会主动表达出来……如果他们没有主动这么做，那很可能已经凭直觉有所察觉。帮助他们将这些想法写下来，使其更具条理性，是开启这场对话的绝佳方式。这就是你可以做的一件事。（01:05:06）：第二件事是，我认为人们往往会因为担心反馈会显得唐突而避免给予反馈。所以不妨主动邀请你的经理说：“看，我真的想提升自己。请随时告诉我你的看法。可以实时反馈，不用字斟句酌，我只想确保自己能不断进步。” 与经理达成这样的共识，并允许他们随时给予反馈，这样能确保反馈的频率大大增加。先从增加反馈的数量入手，逐步提升反馈的质量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As you're talking, I'm thinking of the advice Jules Walter shared on this podcast a couple episodes ago of when you get feedback, no matter how it makes you feel, whether you're melting inside or not, just be very enthusiastically. Thank you so much for that. That was really helpful.
turns.zh: 你讲的时候，我突然想起朱尔斯·沃尔特几期前在播客上分享的建议：无论收到反馈时感觉如何，内心是否崩溃，都要保持热情积极的态度。非常感谢，这建议太实用了。

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: It's so key because then you've rewarded the person for giving you feedback, even if it hurts inside, and then they'll want to do it in the future.
turns.zh: 这很关键，因为这样你就奖励了对方给予反馈的行为，即便反馈内容让你心里难受，他们下次也会更愿意这么做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Anything else that you want to touch on or share before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 是的。在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想补充或分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: One of the challenges I hear PMs that are moving into leadership roles is they often worry about micromanaging their teams. And so I kind of see two failure modes for people that are taking on their first leadership role. The first one is that they do actually micromanage, and so they don't let the person on their team have the autonomy that they need to figure out a path forward. And there's two problems in that, one that really makes that person feel like you don't trust them. The second thing is that rate limits the size of the team that you can manage because you can only do that for a finite set of people before you yourself are tapped out on bandwidth. And it's usually a couple of folks. So that's one failure mode where people sort of treat their first direct reports as an extension of themselves. (01:06:51): The second failure mode that I commonly see is just a completely hands-off mode of leadership where a person assumes that the new person on their team, they trust them, they give them a lot of autonomy, but as part of that, they don't give them the context that they need. So that person may be able to be successful but may actually lack the guard rails and the frameworks to channel their efforts. And so I think the right solution here is to say, actually micromanagement is not a bad thing. Some of the most innovative leaders in tech are famous micromanagers. Steve Jobs is a micromanager. Elon Musk is a micromanager. Mark Zuckerberg's a micromanager. Ultimately as product builders and products innovators, the details matter and sometimes you need to zoom into what does the text on a particular button say, and you might have a strong opinion on that. And so it's okay to engage at that level. (01:07:46): I often encourage product leaders to think about their process of becoming more senior, not as a matter of getting more and more high level, but of increasing their dynamic range. So a CPO, it's not that a CPO never thinks about tactical issues, it's that they spend a lot of time on strategy, but they also can zoom into specific issues. And so a framework I like to use with product leaders that I'm coaching is to think about a matrix. Your ideal goal is to lead in a scalable way, which means you feel really confident about the direction of your team and your team has the autonomy to move in that direction. (01:08:22): There's another really effective way of leading which is selective micromanagement, which if you don't feel confident in the direction that your team is moving, the right answer is not to be hands-off and to let them go in that wrong direction. The right answer is to micromanage, but do it in a very tactical, in a very temporary way so that you can help them understand what is the right direction moving forward, so that you can then pull back. And the two failure modes are if you're hands-off and you let that team go off the rails, that hands-off mode of leadership might feel really good in the short term. It might help you avoid micromanaging in the short term, but ultimately it's going to mean that that team doesn't get to where they need to go. (01:09:03): And then what we commonly think of as micromanagement, I think more of as micro mismanagement, which is you don't feel like you've got a sense of control or a sense of confidence about what the team's doing. The team doesn't feel like they have a sense of autonomy. There's not a clear end in sight, and ultimately both the leader and the team are frustrated. So I think the two really effective functional ways of leading are scalable leadership where the team has autonomy, you have confidence or selective micromanagement where for a brief period of time you might take away some of the team's autonomy to set them on the right track, but with the goal of getting back into that scalable leadership mode.
turns.zh:
我听说，许多初次担任领导角色的产品经理都面临一个挑战——他们往往担心过度微管理团队。基于此，我总结出两种初级领导者容易陷入的失败模式。第一种是真的过度微管理，剥夺了团队成员自主探索前进路径的权限。这种做法有两个问题：一是让团队成员觉得你不信任他们；二是由于你只能同时管理有限数量的人，最终会被团队规模所束缚，通常只能管理几个人。这就是第一种失败模式——把直接下属视为自己的延伸。  

（01:06:51）第二种常见的失败模式是完全放手式领导。这种领导者假定新加入的团队成员值得信任，于是赋予他们大量自主权，但却忽视提供必要的上下文指导。这种方式可能让团队取得短期成功，但却缺乏方向指引。正确的解决方案是承认微管理并非坏事。科技界许多创新型领导者都是著名的微管理者——史蒂夫·乔布斯、埃隆·马斯克、马克·扎克伯格皆是如此。作为产品创新者，细节至关重要，有时你需要仔细检查按钮文案的每个字，并对此提出专业见解。这种深度参与是完全合理的。  

（01:07:46）我常鼓励产品领导者将晋升视为动态能力提升的过程，而非层级攀升。例如，首席产品官（CPO）并非从不关注战术问题，而是将更多精力投入战略规划，同时保持对细节的把控。我常用的一个框架是矩阵思维。理想状态是以可扩展的方式领导团队，即对方向有清晰把握，同时赋予团队自主探索的权限。  

（01:08:22）选择性微管理也是有效策略。当对团队方向缺乏信心时，放任其偏离轨道绝非明智之举。正确做法是以战术性临时微管理来引导团队回归正轨。两种失败模式：放任自流导致团队偏离轨道；过度微管理则让团队失去自主性。  

（01:09:03）所谓微管理，实质是缺乏掌控感与信心。当团队失去自主权，无法预见清晰的终点时，领导者与团队都会陷入挫败感。两种有效领导方式：可扩展领导（赋予团队自主权）与选择性微管理（在关键时刻介入纠偏）。
既有自主权，又要保持信心；或者采用选择性微观管理策略。在短时间内，你可能会暂时剥夺团队的部分自主权，以便让他们走上正确的轨道，但最终目标是重新回归到可扩展的领导模式中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like this topic. I feel like this could be a whole other thread. Maybe one quick question along these lines. Would you call it selective micromanagement?
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢这个话题。我觉得这可以单独开个帖子讨论。或许可以顺便问个相关问题：你会把这称为选择性微管理吗？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a heuristic you have in mind of just like what does that mean in practice? Like one out of every 10 decisions, maybe you push them in a direction that you'd need them to go. How do you figure out what's selective enough or is there in your experience?
turns.zh: 你有没有什么启发性的方法来解释这在实际中意味着什么？比如每10个决策中，你可能就把其中一个往你希望的方向上推。你是如何判断什么样的行为算“选择性”微管理的呢？或者说根据你的经验，有没有相关标准？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: I think it often comes down to being overly detailed at the moment that you see a problem. So helping the team get back on track by any means necessary, including potentially you're getting really detailed about the decisions that the team is making. But as you do that, think about the frameworks that you're using to help the team make decisions and help the team understand that framework. And so over time, the goal is to replace you actively kind of going in and guiding the team's decisions with them having a framework that they really understand so that they can make the decisions that are aligned with where you think the right direction is to go. And the ultimate success is that you give enough of a framework and the team has enough autonomy that they get to answers that are even better than you could come up with. And so that gives the team an incredible feeling of power and that gives you as a leader an incredible feeling of confidence in the team's ability.
turns.zh: 我觉得这通常源于在发现问题时过于关注细节。比如通过各种手段帮助团队重回正轨，包括对团队决策进行过度细致的指导。但在做这些事时，你需要思考用什么框架来帮助团队做决策，并确保他们理解这个框架。最终目标是让团队主动接管决策权，而不是被动接受你的指导。理想情况是，你提供足够的框架，团队凭借自主权做出比你预期的更好的决策。这会给团队带来强大的掌控感，也会让你作为领导者对团队能力充满信心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Yeah. Well, this makes me think about it as a product leader. Most of the time you need to push your team to do the thing that you believe is right, and maybe once in a while let them make a mistake and have them learn from it. But it's not the other way. It's not like, "Cool, let them make all the mistakes and once in a while correct." It's the opposite. Your ass is on the line if they waste time and resources and fail. So yeah, your job is to make sure they're heading in the right direction.
turns.zh: 明白了。作为产品负责人，我觉得你需要推动团队朝着你认为正确的方向前进，可能偶尔让他们犯错并从中学习。但反之则不行。如果他们浪费时间和资源并失败了，责任最终还是落在你头上。所以你的职责就是确保他们朝着正确的方向前进。

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: There's another framework that we talk about in product leadership which goes into this topic, which is as someone who's working with a manager, there's kind of two things that you're constantly solving for. One is the degree to which you're aligned with your manager, and the second is the degree to which your manager has confidence in you. And so if there's a high degree of alignment and a high degree of confidence, you have full support, but there might be cases where there's actually not a high degree of alignment. You want to go in a different direction than your manager wants to go in, but if you have their confidence, you'll get their permission, you'll get their support to go in that direction. (01:11:56): And so keeping an idea of where you are on that radar is really helpful for understanding the currency that you have to be able to push things in the direction that you think is the right one. And if you don't have your leader's confidence and you're not aligned with them, that's not a recipe for success. One of those things needs to change. Either you need to do things that they are aligned with or you need to do things to win their confidence in your ability to pick a different path forward.
turns.zh: 在产品管理中我们还讨论过另一个框架：作为与经理合作的人，你需要不断解决两个问题。一是与经理的目标是否一致，二是经理对你的信任程度。若两者高度一致，你就能获得全力支持；但如果不一致，比如你想走与经理相反的方向，只要得到他们的信任，你就能获得许可和支持。（01:11:56）因此，了解自己在这些维度上的位置，对你能否推动团队朝着正确方向前进至关重要。如果得不到领导的信任或与他们目标不一致，那就注定失败了。其中一项必须改变。要么顺应他们的意愿，要么努力赢得他们对另辟蹊径的信任。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that. One final tangential totally out of nowhere question. I had on my notes that you've been doing some stuff with AI in your coaching work. And so I wanted to ask you, how do you think AI will work with PMs and just coaches and us as, I don't know, professionals in the workplace? What have you found so far in your experience there?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个想法。最后再问一个完全不相干但突然冒出来的问题。我记得你的笔记里提到，你在教练工作中使用了人工智能技术。所以我想问一下，你认为人工智能将如何与项目经理、教练以及我们这些职场人士合作？到目前为止，你在实践中发现了什么？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: So when we started Outpace, we knew that AI was going to continue to advance and that eventually we would want to think about AI as a way to amplify coaches and to help make them more efficient and more effective. We thought that that was going to be a multi-year journey and that we would get to it at some point in the future. But this year's been incredibly exciting with the advances that we've seen from OpenAI and Stable Diffusion and Midjourney and all of these different models. [NEW_PARAGRAPH]And so we've actually accelerated a lot of our roadmap around that. We have an interesting opportunity to use AI in the product where one of the things that makes Outpace different from other coaching platforms is we provide both content as well as the coach. And so each week a person will go through a 20 or 30-minute session. That session includes a brief audio lesson and then includes interactive exercises that go into how would you use the things that you just learned in that lesson. (01:13:42): And so one of the things that we have is we've got text content from all of the participants in Outpace where they're providing very specific answers to very specific questions. We're using that content to prompt, in this case, OpenAI, to give suggestions to the coach. And so the coach can go in and say, "Help me with a suggestion of what I should say as feedback to this particular response." And then the coach can go in and tailor that based on what they know about that person. And one of the most amazing things is we've been able to simulate different styles of leadership by using different types of prompts. So we can have suggestions that are really action oriented that provide lists of next steps. We can have suggestions that are more sympathetic that focus on the person's feelings. We've got suggestions that are more inquisitive, which ask follow-up questions. We've got suggestions which are informative, which provide frameworks and advice. (01:14:32): So it's really pretty remarkable how far the technology has come. I know we're at an interesting time right now. It's going to be interesting to see how things play out. I think one of the most interesting things about it is not AI as a replacement for people, but AI as a way to amplify people and make them more effective. And I think we'll see a lot of that in terms of both image generation and text generation where it's less about AI doing all the work and more about AI providing a really good starting point.
turns.zh: 当我们创立Outpace时，我们就知道人工智能会持续发展，最终我们会将其视为一种增强教练效率和效果的工具。我们原以为这将是一个多年发展的过程，但今年的进展令人振奋——OpenAI、Stable Diffusion和Midjourney等模型的发展速度超出了我们的想象。[新段落]因此，我们已经大大加快了相关路线图的推进。我们有一个有趣的机会，将人工智能应用于产品中。Outpace与其他教练平台的不同之处在于，我们既提供内容也提供教练服务。每周，用户会完成20至30分钟的课程，包括简短的音频课程和互动练习，帮助他们应用刚刚学到的知识。（01:13:42）目前，我们收集了所有Outpace参与者的文本内容，他们提供了针对特定问题的具体答案。我们利用这些内容来引导OpenAI为教练提供建议。例如，教练可以输入“请为这段回应提供反馈建议”，OpenAI会根据用户提供的信息进行个性化回复。最令人惊叹的是，通过不同的提示语，我们可以模拟不同类型的领导风格。比如，提供以行动为导向的建议列表，提供更具同理心的情感支持，提出探索性问题，提供信息性建议等。（01:14:32）技术的发展速度实在令人惊叹。我知道我们正处于一个有趣的阶段。未来会如何发展，将非常值得关注。我认为最有趣的部分不是人工智能取代人类，而是它能增强人类的能力，提高工作效率。这在图像生成和文本生成方面都将得到体现——重点不在于让AI包办一切，而在于为人类提供优质的起点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the idea that people have these visions of where their product's going to go in five, 10 years, and the vision's happening so soon. And that's got to feel nice, but then you got to rethink, "Oh my God, what's our new vision of the future at this pace?"
turns.zh: 我喜欢人们对产品未来五年、十年愿景的构想，而现实进展如此之快。这感觉一定很棒，但随之而来的是重新思考：“天哪，以这样的发展速度，未来我们的新愿景会是什么？”

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: It's been really exciting. I haven't been this excited about tech in a long time. And I think it was, we knew we would need to pivot in order to embrace this more, but it completely makes sense and it fits really nicely into something that we're already doing.
turns.zh: 整个过程非常激动人心。我已经很久没有对科技如此兴奋了。我们知道需要调整方向以更好地拥抱这种变化，但这一切都顺理成章，与我们现有的工作方向完美契合。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you. I'm going to power through them and whatever comes to mind, just share it away. Sound good?
turns.zh: 好的，接下来我们要进行激动人心的闪电问答环节。我准备了六个问题，大家可以畅所欲言。听起来不错吧？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: That sounds good.
turns.zh: 听起来很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. What are two or three books that you recommend most to other people?
turns.zh: 太好了。你最推荐给别人的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: I really like Hooked. That's a book that I know came out a few years ago, but I find that that model is just such an effective model for thinking about how to create products that are engaging. I also really like Working Backwards. I think Amazon has such a unique way of going about building product, and they've been so opinionated about what matters within that process. It's great to get a really detailed window into that. I was always curious about how it worked, and Working Backwards was a great way too to understand that a lot better.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢《上瘾》。这本书几年前出版的，但我发现里面提到的产品设计模型，对打造引人入胜的产品非常有效。我还很喜欢《倒退工作法》。亚马逊在产品开发方面有独特的思路，他们对产品开发流程中的关键环节也极具洞察力。能深入了解他们的方法真是太棒了。我一直很好奇他们的运作模式，《倒退工作法》让我对此有了更清晰的认识。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For folks that are interested in that, we had Ian McAllister on the podcast talking a lot about that stuff. So if you're interested in Working Backwards and don't want to read the book, there's a podcast episode for you. Speaking of podcast, what's a favorite other podcast of yours other than the one you're currently on?
turns.zh: 对感兴趣的人来说，我们在播客上邀请了伊恩·麦卡利斯特详细探讨过这些内容。所以如果你对《倒退工作法》感兴趣但不想读原书，播客节目会是很好的选择。说到播客，除了你现在参与的播客，还有其他喜欢的吗？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: Yeah. One of my favorites is The Ezra Klein Show. I love the fact that he talks about a bunch of different topics. He's often got contrarian points of view. He just had an episode recently about a skeptical take on AI that I disagreed with a lot, but it was really interesting to think about it from a different perspective.
turns.zh: 是的。我最喜欢的播客之一是《埃兹拉·克莱恩秀》。我喜欢他探讨各种不同话题的风格。他经常提出一些反主流观点，最近他做了一期关于人工智能的怀疑论，我虽然不认同，但从不同角度思考这个问题还是很有趣的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of the best compliments I got about this podcast is someone telling me that they listened to these two podcasts as the only two podcasts they listen to, and they always have to pick one or the other when they're going in their morning walk. [inaudible 01:16:45].
turns.zh: 我收到过的最好的赞美之一，是有人告诉我，他们把你的播客和《埃兹拉·克莱恩秀》作为唯一收听的两个播客，每天晨跑时总要在两者中二选一。[1:16:45未录音]

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: You and I were talking a few months ago, and that's sort of the boat that I'm in. I've been listening to your podcast. I've been listening to Ezra Klein, and then there's a couple of others that are in the mix, but the ones that I keep going back to when I'm walking the dog are those two podcasts.
turns.zh: 几个月前我们聊天时，我也处于类似的境况。我一直在听你的播客，也听埃兹拉的节目，还有其他几档，但晨跑时反复回听的还是这两个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a dream.
turns.zh: 真是梦想成真了。

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: Thanks for having me on.
turns.zh: 感谢邀请我参加节目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man. It's not over yet. Next question. Favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 天哪，还没结束呢。下一个问题：你最近最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: I love Andor. I just finished watching it about a week ago. I think it's not just a great Star Wars piece of content, it's just a really great piece of science fiction. I think a lot of science fiction has gotten very samey and very dystopian recently. This was such an interesting reflection of what's happening today, really deep thinking about what the future could look like, really good expansion of the universe. So it's just great on a lot of levels.
turns.zh: 我超爱《安多》。我大约一周前刚看完。我觉得它不仅是《星球大战》系列的佳作，更是优秀的科幻作品。最近很多科幻作品都千篇一律、充斥反乌托邦题材，而这部作品对当下现实的反思深刻，对未来可能性的思考也颇具深度，宇宙观的拓展也非常出色。真是各方面都超棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Frigging love Andor. Huge plus one on that. Favorite interview question that you like to ask.
turns.zh: 我太爱《安多》了！强烈推荐！最喜欢问的采访问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: My favorite interview question is, tell me about a product that you love. And I can have that question last five minutes. I can have that question last 60 minutes. And so that's the first question that I'll typically ask people during a screening interview. I use the word love very deliberately. I want to see what products in their lives they really gravitate to and they engage with and that they can use that word with. That helps me understand a lot about what they value. And then I'll ask a whole series of questions, which is, why do you love it? Why do you think other people love it? What would you like to see about it in the future? Pick a feature that you'd like to build for that product. Why do you think that's a good feature? How would you measure the success of that feature? (01:18:11): So I've used this for years. It's just such a good way to help understand the product sense that a person has, help get to know a person a little bit better. It's always interesting when people pick products that are more physical products to see what they're into in terms of hobbies and things of that sort.
turns.zh:
我最喜欢的面试问题是，告诉我你喜欢的一款产品。我可以让这个问题持续五分钟，也能让它延续60分钟。这通常是我在筛选面试中最先问候的问题。我特意使用“喜欢”这个词，是想看看他们生活中真正热衷并深度参与的那些产品，以及他们能用这个词来形容的产品。这能让我更好地理解他们的价值观。接下来我会追问一系列问题：你为什么喜欢它？你觉得其他人为什么会喜欢它？你希望未来能看到哪些改进？你想为这款产品开发哪项功能？你为什么认为这项功能很棒？又该如何衡量其成功效果？（01:18:11）  
多年来我一直用这个方法。这是了解候选人产品敏感度、深入了解他们的绝佳途径。当有人选择实体产品时，我会格外感兴趣，借此探究他们的兴趣爱好等深层特质。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are five SaaS products that you use at your company or on your team?
turns.zh: 你们公司或团队使用的五款SaaS产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: Airtable has been amazing. It's such a powerful tool. We just rebuilt our accounting system in Airtable. Webflow, we're using constantly. It's really changed how we think about building products. We now ask, do we need to build code or can we do something in Webflow? We're using Superhuman. I spend most of my day in Superhuman. It's an incredibly fast email client, so I love having it on my team. A lot of the team today is using Descript or Descript to edit videos. They found that to be something that works so much better than prior audio and video editing solutions. And then I've always loved Balsamiq. I've been a Balsamiq user for probably 10 years now, and whenever I get stuck on a user experience issue, I go in, I create some wireframes, and it always helps.
turns.zh: Airtable太棒了。它是个强大的工具。我们刚用Airtable重建了会计系统。Webflow我们一直在用，它彻底改变了我们的产品开发思路。我们现在会问：是需要写代码，还是能在Webflow里实现？Superhuman是我日常主要使用的邮件客户端。Descript/Descript被我们用来剪辑视频。他们发现这个工具比以往的音频和视频编辑解决方案好用太多了。Balsamiq我也一直爱用，使用了大概10年。每当我在用户体验方面卡壳时，就会用它快速创建线框图，效果总是很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We use Descript/Descript, I also don't know how to pronounce it, on this podcast. So a huge recommend of that. Final question. You are building a company that is helping people find coaches. Do you have any tips for someone that is talking to a potential coach and what they should maybe ask them when they're trying to decide if it would be a good fit?
turns.zh: 我们播客用的就是Descript/Descript，我也不知道怎么发音。强烈推荐这个工具。最后一个问题。你正在打造一个帮助人们寻找教练的公司，对于那些正在与潜在教练沟通的人，你有什么建议？在判断是否合适时，他们应该问些什么？

turns.speaker: Ravi Mehta
turns.en: Yeah. I think one of the questions that's really helpful is tell me about the client that you're most proud of helping. What was the challenge if they were facing? How did you help them meet that challenge? The person doesn't need to go into anything confidential, of course, but I think what's really nice about that question is it get you really deep insight into what they value. You get to see where their pride comes from. It gives you insight into how they engage with the people that they're helping. And then you can understand, does that sort of map with what you're looking for in terms of a coach?
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得一个很有用的问题是，告诉我你最引以为傲帮助过的客户。他们面临的挑战是什么？你如何帮助他们克服这些挑战？当然，候选人无需透露任何机密信息。但这个问题的好处在于，能让你深入了解他们的价值观，看到他们的自豪感从何而来。这能让你了解他们如何与受助者互动。然后你就能判断，这是否与你对教练的期望相契合？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ravi, this was everything I hoped it would be. I learned a lot. I had a lot of fun. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to learn more, and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 拉维，这次访谈完全符合我的期待。我收获满满，乐趣无穷。最后两个问题：如果读者想了解更多信息，哪里能找到你的信息？听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.en: My startup is Outpace. You can find it at outpace.co. We published a lot of free resources. We just published a resource that you helped us with, Lenny, called Unlock Your Product Manager Potential. We also have a Q and A service where you can ask questions of coaches. Our goal with Outpace is to get more and more people to experience coaching, whether that's in an active coaching relationship or just a really quick conversation with a coach. So come to outpace.co. That'll be really helpful for us and hopefully really helpful for you as well. And then if you want to follow me, I'm on LinkedIn. You can also read my writing at ravi-mehta.com.
turns.zh: 我的创业公司叫Outpace，网址是outpace.co。我们发布了大量免费资源。最近刚上线了一份由Lenny协助制作的资源，名为《释放你的产品经理潜力》。我们还提供问答服务，用户可以向导师提问。Outpace的目标是让越来越多的人体验到教练指导，无论是通过深度合作关系，还是与导师进行快速交流。所以请访问outpace.co吧。这对我们和大家都将非常有益。另外，如果想关注我，我在LinkedIn上有账号，也欢迎访问ravi-mehta.com阅读我的文章。

turns.en: Amazing. Ravi, again, thank you for being here, and we'll share all these in the show notes and all these links you mentioned. Thanks again.
